name: Corticospinal tract (lateral)
modality: Somatic motor — voluntary skilled movement, especially fine fractionated control of distal limbs
origin: Layer V neurons of primary motor, premotor, supplementary motor and somatosensory/parietal cortex; fibres descend through corona radiata, posterior limb of internal capsule, basis pedunculi, ventral pons and medullary pyramids.
target: Contralateral spinal interneurons and anterior horn motor neurons after pyramidal crossing, with a major role in distal limb and skilled hand movement.
decussation: Most fibres (approximately 85-90%, with individual variation) cross at the caudal medullary pyramidal decussation to form the lateral tract. Anterior corticospinal fibres are a separate, mainly axial pathway with bilateral/segmental projections.
somatotopy: Cortical and supraspinal motor organization is topographic. The atlas has no validated human spinal lamination: a fixed cervical-medial/sacral-lateral map should not be inferred from its schematic tube or used as a localization rule.
function: Major descending pathway for voluntary limb movement, especially fractionated distal movements. Injury may produce weakness and upper motor neuron signs; acute lesions can initially cause reduced tone and reflexes.

clinical.syndrome: Corticospinal lesion above the pyramidal decussation
clinical.findings: Contralateral limb weakness; associated face weakness requires corticobulbar involvement. Capsular injury can produce a pure motor syndrome, but the pattern depends on lesion extent.
Ipsilateral upper motor neuron weakness below the lesion; a hemicord lesion also affects other sensory and motor pathways.

name: Corticobulbar tract
modality: Somatic/branchiomotor — voluntary control of cranial-nerve motor nuclei (facial expression, mastication, tongue, palate, larynx)
origin: Lower lateral precentral gyrus (face/tongue area) and adjacent frontal operculum → genu of the internal capsule → medial crus cerebri
target: Brainstem motor nuclei controlling jaw, face, pharynx, larynx and tongue, directly or via interneurons. Cortical control of ocular movements uses additional supranuclear gaze networks.
decussation: Projections cross at several brainstem levels and are predominantly bilateral. Lower facial motor neurons and genioglossus receive important contralateral input; this is not a single compact decussation.
somatotopy: Orofacial representation lies mainly in inferolateral motor cortex; descending fibres pass through the genu/adjacent internal capsule. Brainstem projections are distributed rather than a precisely mapped single tube.
function: Contributes to voluntary orofacial, swallowing and speech movements through cranial motor networks. Bilateral innervation gives partial redundancy, with clinically important exceptions.

clinical.findings: Often contralateral lower facial weakness with relative forehead sparing; forehead sparing is a useful pattern, not an absolute diagnostic rule.
May cause pseudobulbar dysarthria, dysphagia, brisk jaw reflex and emotional lability.
May impair contralateral genioglossus; protruded tongue can deviate toward the weak side, away from a unilateral cortical lesion. Bilateral innervation can limit the deficit.

name: Corticopontine tract
modality: Corticocerebellar relay — conveys cortical motor planning and associative signals to the pontine nuclei
origin: Widespread neocortex: frontopontine fibers from frontal lobe (medial crus), temporoparietooccipitopontine fibers from posterior cortex (lateral crus)
target: Ipsilateral pontine nuclei. Their separate pontocerebellar axons cross in the pons and enter the opposite cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle.
decussation: Corticopontine fibres themselves principally terminate ipsilaterally. Crossing belongs to the downstream pontocerebellar projection, not to this tract.
somatotopy: In the crus cerebri the frontopontine component is most medial and the temporoparietooccipitopontine component most lateral, flanking the corticobulbar and corticospinal bundles
function: Relays widespread cortical information to pontine nuclei, forming the input limb of corticopontocerebellar circuits involved in coordination and motor learning.

clinical.findings: Supratentorial or pontine injury can contribute to ataxia, often together with weakness or other deficits. Side depends on the site relative to the crossed pontocerebellar projection; an isolated tract syndrome is difficult to establish.

name: Rubrospinal tract
modality: Descending somatic motor pathway; human functional contribution is limited and uncertain, and animal flexor-control mechanisms do not establish a human rule.
origin: Magnocellular (caudal) division of the red nucleus in the midbrain.
target: Mainly cervical spinal interneurons in humans; the pathway is much smaller than in many experimental animals.
decussation: Crosses soon after leaving the red nucleus at the ventral tegmental decussation (Forel) in the midbrain.
somatotopy: No precise human somatotopic map is represented here.
function: A descending lateral motor pathway with an uncertain and relatively limited role in humans. Animal flexor-control mechanisms should not be treated as a complete explanation of human movement or posturing.

clinical.findings: Posturing can occur with severe hemispheric or brainstem injury. Classical rubrospinal explanations are teaching models and do not establish the exact lesion level or prognosis in an individual.

name: Tectospinal tract
modality: Reflex somatic motor — orienting reflexes of head and neck toward visual (and multimodal) stimuli
origin: Deep layers of the superior colliculus, integrating sensory signals relevant to orienting.
target: Mainly cervical spinal interneurons involved in head and neck orientation.
decussation: Crosses in the dorsal tegmental decussation (Meynert) in the midbrain, then descends near the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
somatotopy: This illustration does not resolve a human somatotopic map.
function: Participates in orienting head/neck movements toward sensory stimuli. Its isolated clinical contribution in humans is uncertain.

clinical.findings: Head/eye orienting abnormalities may accompany collicular or brainstem network lesions; a characteristic isolated human tectospinal syndrome is not established.

name: Lateral vestibulospinal tract
modality: Postural somatic motor — antigravity extensor facilitation driven by the otolith organs
origin: Lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters) near the pontomedullary region.
target: Ipsilateral spinal interneurons throughout the cord, influencing axial/proximal and antigravity muscles.
decussation: Predominantly uncrossed descent; downstream spinal networks have broader bilateral interactions.
somatotopy: Runs in the ventral funiculus of the cord; lamination axial-proximal, influencing extensor tone from cervical to sacral levels
function: Uses vestibular information to help maintain posture and balance, including facilitation of extensor/antigravity activity.

clinical.findings: Brainstem injury involving vestibular nuclei and descending pathways may contribute to imbalance and falling; vertigo and nystagmus involve additional vestibular circuits.
A peripheral vestibular nerve disorder can alter vestibulospinal drive secondarily; it does not imply a lesion of the Deiters nucleus.

name: Medial vestibulospinal tract
modality: Head/neck postural reflex motor — semicircular-canal-driven stabilization of head position
origin: Mainly medial vestibular nucleus, with contributions from the inferior vestibular nucleus.
target: Bilateral cervical and upper thoracic spinal interneurons controlling head and neck muscles.
decussation: Contains crossed and uncrossed projections, descending bilaterally in association with the medial longitudinal fasciculus (descending MLF).
somatotopy: Predominantly head/neck control, without a validated fine somatotopic map in this illustration.
function: Supports vestibulocollic reflexes and stabilization of head position. Ascending vestibulo-ocular fibres are related but have different targets.

clinical.findings: May impair head stabilization and postural responses. Clinical vestibular signs cannot usually be assigned to this tract alone.

name: Reticulospinal tract (pontine and medullary)
modality: Descending somatic motor/postural networks; contributions to muscle tone, locomotion and coordinated movement.
origin: Pontine and medullary reticular formation, containing heterogeneous descending neuronal populations.
target: Spinal interneurons and motor neurons across multiple segments, with substantial bilateral influence.
decussation: Distributed crossed and uncrossed projections; no single obligatory decussation.
somatotopy: Broad medial motor-system influence on axial/proximal muscles; no precise human map is modeled.
function: Contributes to posture, gait, anticipatory adjustments and voluntary movements. A simple pontine-excitatory/medullary-inhibitory split does not capture the full system.

clinical.findings: Reticulospinal circuits may contribute to residual movement and abnormal synergies after corticospinal injury; these outcomes involve multiple descending and spinal mechanisms.
Often causes mixed motor/postural deficits; isolated reticulospinal lesions are difficult to identify clinically.

name: Medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)
modality: Internuclear oculomotor and vestibular — conjugate gaze coordination and vestibulo-ocular/vestibulocollic integration
origin: Vestibular nuclei and brainstem ocular motor internuclear neurons; horizontal gaze interneurons arise in the abducens nucleus.
target: Oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nuclei, linking conjugate eye movements and vestibulo-ocular responses.
decussation: Abducens internuclear axons cross in the pons soon after leaving the abducens nucleus, then ascend in the opposite MLF to medial-rectus neurons of CN III. Other MLF components include crossed and uncrossed vestibular projections.
somatotopy: Paired paramedian bundle in the dorsal tegmentum: floor of the fourth ventricle through the pons, just ventral to the periaqueductal gray in the midbrain, continuing caudally into the cervical medial longitudinal bundle
function: Coordinates ocular motor nuclei with one another and with vestibular inputs. It is a mixed internuclear bundle rather than a single sensory or motor tract.

clinical.findings: Impaired adduction of the eye ipsilateral to the MLF lesion during horizontal gaze, often with contralateral abducting nystagmus. Convergence is frequently preserved, but not always.
An ipsilateral MLF lesion plus abducens-nucleus or PPRF damage causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy and INO; only contralateral eye abduction remains horizontally.

name: Central tegmental tract
modality: Motor-coordination loop (rubro-olivary fibers of the Guillain–Mollaret triangle) plus ascending/descending reticular fibers
origin: Includes descending fibres from the parvocellular (rostral) red nucleus; other ascending/reticular fibres occupy the central tegmental region.
target: Ipsilateral inferior olivary nucleus for the descending rubro-olivary component.
decussation: The rubro-olivary component is principally uncrossed. Dentatorubral input crosses via the superior cerebellar peduncle; olivocerebellar output crosses to the opposite cerebellar cortex via the inferior peduncle.
somatotopy: No fine somatotopic representation is provided.
function: The rubro-olivary component forms part of the dentato-rubro-olivary circuit. The return route involves olivary climbing fibres to cerebellar cortex and deep-nuclear circuitry, not a simple direct olive-to-dentate synapse.

clinical.findings: Interruption of afferent connections to the olive can cause delayed ipsilateral olivary degeneration after central tegmental injury, sometimes with palatal/oculopalatal tremor. Not every affected patient has tremor; isolated olivocerebellar output injury does not produce the same deafferentation pattern.

name: Hypothalamospinal (sympathetic) tract
modality: Visceromotor — descending sympathetic (and hypothalamic autonomic) control of preganglionic sympathetic neurons
origin: Hypothalamic autonomic regions, including pathways descending through the lateral brainstem.
target: Spinal sympathetic preganglionic neurons. The oculosympathetic component reaches upper thoracic intermediolateral neurons (chiefly T1-T2), then sympathetic chain and superior cervical ganglion.
decussation: The clinically localized descending oculosympathetic pathway is mainly ipsilateral; broader hypothalamic autonomic projections are distributed.
somatotopy: Lateral brainstem descent is a teaching localization, not a precisely delimited fibre bundle or fine map.
function: Descending autonomic control includes sympathetic drive to the pupil, eyelid smooth muscle and sweating through a three-neuron oculosympathetic chain.

clinical.findings: Ipsilateral miosis, mild ptosis and variable anhidrosis can accompany lateral brainstem or spinal injury. Horner syndrome also has peripheral preganglionic/postganglionic causes.

With intact postganglionic terminals, hydroxyamphetamine can dilate a central or preganglionic Horner pupil; dilation is reduced in a postganglionic lesion. Timing and other limitations prevent this from being an absolute rule.
clinical.note: Educational mechanism, not a recommendation for self-testing or a substitute for clinical assessment.

name: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway
modality: Somatic sensory — discriminative (fine) touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, two-point discrimination
origin: Large-fibre dorsal-root ganglion neurons ascend ipsilaterally in gracile/cuneate fasciculi and relay in the corresponding caudal medullary nuclei.
target: Contralateral VPL thalamus via medial lemniscus, then primary somatosensory cortex. Facial sensory relays use separate trigeminal pathways and VPM.
decussation: Second-order axons cross in the caudal medulla as internal arcuate fibres (sensory decussation).
somatotopy: Dorsal columns: lower body medial (gracile), upper body lateral (cuneate). Medial lemniscus: feet more ventral in medulla; arms more medial and legs more lateral in pons/midbrain as the ribbon rotates. These are broad teaching relationships.
function: Conveys vibration, conscious proprioception and discriminative touch from the body.

clinical.findings: Ipsilateral vibration/proprioception loss below a spinal lesion; sensory ataxia may worsen without visual guidance.
Contralateral body vibration/proprioception loss above the sensory crossing, such as in medial medullary infarction.

clinical.syndrome: Tabes dorsalis and other large-fibre disorders
clinical.findings: Tabes dorsalis is neurosyphilitic disease of dorsal roots/columns. B12 deficiency and peripheral large-fibre neuropathies can also impair these modalities but are separate diagnoses.

name: Spinothalamic tract (anterolateral system)
modality: Somatic sensory — sharp/fast pain, thermal sense, crude (non-discriminative) touch and pressure; salient affective pain components
origin: Spinal dorsal horn projection neurons, particularly laminae I and V, after primary afferents enter and may travel briefly in Lissauer tract.
target: Contralateral thalamus, including VPL and additional medial/intralaminar targets; cortical processing is distributed.
decussation: Most second-order axons cross through the spinal anterior white commissure, often within one or a few segments of entry. Ascending brainstem fibres already represent the opposite body side.
somatotopy: Classical spinal teaching map places sacral fibres relatively lateral and cervical fibres relatively medial; do not treat this as an exact, invariant lamination throughout the brainstem.
function: Major component of the anterolateral system conveying body pain and temperature; related pathways also contribute to crude touch, affective and arousal components.

clinical.findings: Contralateral pain/temperature loss often begins below the injured segment because afferents travel and cross over several segments.

Early syringomyelia can interrupt crossing pain/temperature fibres, causing bilateral segmental sensory loss with relative preservation of posterior-column modalities; larger lesions affect other functions.
Contralateral body pain/temperature loss may accompany ipsilateral face sensory loss from spinal trigeminal involvement.

name: Ventral trigeminothalamic tract
modality: Somatic sensory — face/head touch, pain, temperature, and orofacial proprioceptive relay
origin: Second-order neurons in principal sensory and spinal trigeminal nuclei, receiving predominantly ipsilateral facial/oral afferents.
target: Mainly contralateral VPM thalamus, followed by the face region of somatosensory cortex.
decussation: Fibres cross within the brainstem after their trigeminal nuclear relay; principal and spinal nuclear contributions cross at different levels. Oral touch also has an uncrossed dorsal pathway.
somatotopy: Facial sensory organization varies across nuclei and levels; an exact onion-skin map is not established for this whole ascending bundle.
function: Conveys facial/oral somatosensation, including touch and pain/temperature through different trigeminal nuclear contributions.

clinical.findings: May reduce contralateral facial sensation. In a typical lateral medullary/pontine lesion, ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss instead reflects spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract involvement before crossing.

name: Dorsal trigeminothalamic tract
modality: Somatic sensory — ipsilateral oral-facial mechanoreception (fine touch/pressure of mouth and teeth)
origin: A smaller population of principal (chief) trigeminal sensory nucleus neurons in the pons.
target: Ipsilateral VPM thalamus, particularly for oral tactile/pressure information.
decussation: Uncrossed projection, accompanying the larger crossed ventral trigeminal route.
somatotopy: No validated fine map is represented; the textbook describes oral-cavity touch and dental pressure contributions.
function: A smaller ipsilateral route contributing to bilateral representation of oral somatosensation.

clinical.findings: Bilateral/parallel projections can limit deficits. A reproducible isolated dorsal trigeminothalamic clinical syndrome is not established.

name: Posterior spinocerebellar tract
modality: Unconscious proprioception — lower trunk/lower limb muscle-spindle and Golgi-tendon-organ signals to the cerebellum
origin: Clarke column neurons in caudal cervical/thoracic to upper lumbar cord (commonly described approximately C8/T1-L2/L3), receiving lower-body proprioceptive and other sensory inputs.
target: Ipsilateral cerebellar vermis/intermediate cortex through the inferior cerebellar peduncle, ending as mossy fibres.
decussation: Principally uncrossed throughout the classic dorsal spinocerebellar route.
somatotopy: Occupies the dorsal periphery of the lateral funiculus, superficial to the corticospinal fibers and dorsal to the spinothalamic/anterior spinocerebellar bundles
function: Provides cerebellar feedback about lower-limb/trunk movement and proprioceptive state; does not mediate conscious position sense.

clinical.findings: Can contribute to ipsilateral limb/gait ataxia, typically with other cerebellar pathway injury. Conscious sensory loss depends on involvement of additional pathways.
Ipsilateral ataxia commonly reflects inferior cerebellar peduncle/spinocerebellar involvement.

name: Anterior spinocerebellar tract
modality: Unconscious proprioception — lower-limb locomotor integration (spinal interneuronal state) to the cerebellum
origin: Spinal border and intermediate-zone neurons, especially in lumbosacral cord, integrating spinal interneuronal activity.
target: Predominantly ipsilateral cerebellar representation relative to the side of origin, through a largely double-crossed route entering the superior cerebellar peduncle.
decussation: First crosses in the spinal ventral/anterior white commissure. Many fibres recross on entering/within the cerebellum after traversing the superior cerebellar peduncle; this is not the caudal-midbrain decussation of cerebellar output fibres.
somatotopy: Ascends near the peripheral anterolateral cord/brainstem before joining the superior peduncle; exact fibre ordering is not represented.
function: Reports integrated spinal motor/interneuronal activity to the cerebellum, complementing dorsal spinocerebellar sensory feedback.

clinical.findings: May contribute to ipsilateral ataxia. Clinical lesions usually involve multiple pathways, so this tract is not reliably isolated by examination.

name: Auditory pathway (cochlear nuclei to MGN)
modality: Special sensory — audition, tonotopically organized at every relay
origin: Cochlear nuclei receiving spiral-ganglion afferents through the cochlear division of CN VIII.
target: Bilateral brainstem auditory relays and inferior colliculi, then MGN and auditory cortex through auditory radiations.
decussation: Multiple crossing and uncrossed projections, including trapezoid-body routes in caudal pons. Connections above the cochlear nuclei are bilateral, often with contralateral predominance.
somatotopy: Tonotopic organization occurs at several relays; the exact frequency gradients differ between subnuclei and are not represented by this single curve.
function: Composite teaching route through cochlear nuclei, superior olivary complex/lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus and MGN. It is a branched network: not every fibre obligatorily passes through every depicted relay.

clinical.findings: Can cause ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Vestibular schwannoma is one cause, alongside many cochlear, nerve and brainstem conditions.
May cause acute ipsilateral hearing loss with vestibular or lateral pontine signs, depending on labyrinthine/cochlear pathway involvement.

A unilateral lesion above cochlear nuclei rarely causes complete unilateral deafness; sound localization and temporal processing may be impaired. Bilateral injury can cause severe central hearing impairment.

name: Spinoreticular tract
modality: Nociceptive/visceroceptive arousal — slow dull-aching pain and interoceptive drive to the reticular activating system
origin: Projection neurons distributed in spinal intermediate-zone/ventral-horn laminae VI-VIII, within the broader anterolateral system.
target: Medullary/pontine reticular formation, with onward projections to intralaminar/medial thalamus and distributed forebrain networks.
decussation: Crossed and uncrossed spinal projections give bilateral influence; no single obligatory crossing applies to the composite route.
somatotopy: Diffuse convergence rather than a precise somatotopic map in this illustration.
function: Contributes to affective, autonomic and arousal components of nociception. It is one input to broader arousal networks, not the sole pathway maintaining consciousness.

clinical.findings: Pain experience and alertness involve multiple pathways. An isolated spinoreticular lesion is not an established cause of coma or a distinct reliably localized post-stroke pain syndrome.

name: Optic radiation
modality: Special sensory — vision, retinotopically organized for the contralateral half-field
origin: Lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus: parvocellular and magnocellular relay layers (plus koniocellular layers) receiving crossed nasal and uncrossed temporal retinal fibres
target: Primary visual cortex (V1, striate cortex) around the calcarine fissure — lower-field (superior retinal) fibres to the cuneus above the fissure, upper-field (inferior retinal) fibres to the lingual gyrus below it
decussation: No additional crossing in LGN or optic radiation. Nasal retinal fibres crossed at the optic chiasm; each radiation carries the contralateral visual hemifield.
somatotopy: Temporal Meyer loop carries superior-field information to the inferior bank of calcarine cortex; parietal fibres carry inferior-field information to the superior bank. Central vision has a large posterior cortical representation. Neither this schematic tube nor field congruity establishes a precise individual fibre map.
function: Geniculocalcarine fibres link LGN to striate cortex through retrolenticular internal capsule and temporal/parietal white matter. The displayed curve summarizes a fan-shaped system with distinct branches.

clinical.findings: May cause contralateral superior homonymous quadrantanopia. Anterior extent varies between individuals; there is no universal safe resection distance from the temporal pole.
May cause contralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia; additional reading, sensory or attentional problems depend on associated cortical injury.
May cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Field congruity tends to increase posteriorly but is not a definitive lesion-localization rule.

name: Cingulum
modality: Association (limbic) — bidirectional cortical-cortical fibres of the cingulate and parahippocampal circuit
origin: Distributed cingulate, retrosplenial and adjacent medial cortical regions; association fibres enter and leave along the bundle.
target: Other medial cortical areas and parahippocampal/entorhinal regions through supracallosal and temporal portions.
decussation: No obligatory midline crossing: principally an intrahemispheric association bundle. Interhemispheric communication uses additional commissural pathways.
somatotopy: Topographic association bundle curving around the corpus callosum and continuing toward parahippocampal white matter; not all axons traverse its entire length.
function: Connects medial association and limbic cortices, contributing to attention, memory and affective networks. Its parahippocampal connections form part of the classical Papez teaching circuit.

clinical.findings: May contribute to memory, attention or motivational impairment. These deficits depend on wider network damage and are not uniquely diagnostic of cingulum interruption.

name: Uncinate fasciculus
modality: Association — bidirectional fibres linking the anterior temporal lobe with the orbitofrontal and ventrolateral frontal cortex (ventral semantic and social-emotional stream)
origin: Temporal pole, anterior superior and middle temporal gyrus, and the uncinate/amygdalar region at the anterior temporal stem
target: Orbital and inferior (ventrolateral) frontal cortex, including the lateral orbitofrontal and inferior frontal gyri, hooking around the limen insulae at the anterior inferior insula
decussation: Principally intrahemispheric; curves around the limen insulae between anterior temporal and orbitofrontal regions.
somatotopy: Hook-shaped association bundle; no simple body map. Group-level asymmetry depends on the measurement method and should not be taught as invariably larger on the left.
function: Connects anterior temporal and inferior/orbital frontal regions, contributing to memory, semantic and social-affective processing within broader networks.

clinical.findings: Can contribute to naming, semantic or social-affective impairment. Effects vary with dominance, lesion extent and associated cortical/network injury; a fixed left/right syndrome is not established.
Uncinate abnormalities can occur in frontotemporal and other disorders, but are not selective or diagnostic of one clinical phenotype.

name: Superior longitudinal fasciculus
modality: Association — bidirectional frontoparietal pathways for attention, working memory and sensorimotor integration; relationships to the arcuate depend on anatomical naming convention.
origin: Frontal association/premotor regions linked with parietal cortex by frontoparietal SLF branches.
target: Superior/inferior parietal association regions; nearby arcuate frontotemporal fibres are related but distinguished in many modern anatomical classifications.
decussation: Principally intrahemispheric association connections; reciprocal network traffic has no obligatory midline crossing.
somatotopy: Common classifications distinguish SLF I, II and III. The arcuate fasciculus is sometimes grouped with the SLF system and sometimes treated separately; one curve does not resolve these branches.
function: Frontoparietal association pathways support attention, working memory and sensorimotor integration. Related arcuate/dorsal language connections contribute to speech repetition and auditory-motor mapping.

clinical.syndrome: Conduction aphasia and dorsal language injury
clinical.findings: Dominant perisylvian cortical/subcortical damage can produce fluent paraphasic speech and impaired repetition with relatively preserved comprehension; this is not invariably an isolated arcuate lesion.
Right frontoparietal network disconnection can contribute to left hemispatial neglect; cortical and other white matter lesions also contribute.
